newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk secularists strike back at fallen Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Turk secularists strike back at fallen Islamists.

text.p: Turkey's secularists hit back at the previous Islamist-led government on Tuesday, the first full day in power for new Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz's coalition of anti-Islamists.
The country's top prosecutor urged an investigation into the Islamists' ally, Tansu Ciller, on charges she had accepted money from abroad to work against Turkey's national interests.
And the new culture minister put on hold plans to restore a disused mosque that had become a symbol of a struggle between religious activism and Turkey's secular tradition.

Key leftist leader Deniz Baykal called on former prime minister Necmettin Erbakan's Welfare Party to be brought to account for mixing religion with politics and doing little to clean up a security scandal.
"Welfare cannot leave the table without paying the bill," warned Baykal, leader of one of the leftist parties backing the new anti-Islamist coalition.

Anatolian news agency said Ankara state security court would probe allegations by a far-left leader that conservative Ciller had accepted "money and benefits from foreigners with the intention of acting against the national interest".

Secularists, including the army, have condemned U.S.-educated economist Ciller for joining Erbakan in coalition last year after vowing not to do so. The chief prosecutor, Vural Savas, has also asked the constitutional court to ban Welfare for allegedly threatening NATO member Turkey's secular system.
Turkish financial markets were subdued, with the Istanbul bourse closing 0.32 percent lower on Tuesday after a period of volatility since the last government collapsed.
Erbakan resigned last month under pressure from the generals to crack down on Islamist activism after Welfare announced a series of mostly symbolic challenges to secularism.
The staunchly secular armed forces also received a boost in their campaign against religious radicalism from the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.
The court on Tuesday upheld the air force's forced retirement in 1990 of an officer accused of Islamic fundamentalist beliefs, ruling that his religious freedom had not been violated.

And in the swinging seaside resort of Bodrum, new Culture Minister Istemihan Talay halted an attempt begun by his Islamist predecessor to move an archaeological museum out of a disused mosque in Bodrum Castle.
"The order to move the exhibition has been stopped temporarily while the minister looks into the matter," a spokesman told Reuters.
He said the previous Welfare Party minister had planned to emphasise the "religious identity" of the mosque, originally a Christian chapel.
Erbakan, however, predicted the new government could not win the vote of confidence. Parliament on Tuesday approved holding the vote on July 12.
"In 12 days parliament will fulfil a historic duty, it will turn its back on anti-democratic forces," he told his Welfare deputies in parliament.
Yilmaz's right-left coalition, helped by a stream of resignations from Ciller's party, has on paper enough support to win the confidence of NATO-member Turkey's 550-seat assembly.
Erbakan also railed at planned government reforms which would allow greater state control over religious education.
"This is reactionary. It's like going back to 1945," he said, referring to a period of secularist one-party rule that ended with the introduction of multi-party elections in 1946.
